analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month for people 26 and younger on private health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2025 with 9 Democratic cosponsors and referred to three House committees, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the laws governing private health insurance, employer plans, and catastrophic marketplace plans so that for anyone enrolled who is 26 or younger, health plans must cover at least one insulin of each type and dosage form, charge no deductible for it, and charge no more than $35 per 30-day supply (or 25% of the net negotiated price, whichever is lower). It was introduced in April 2025 and referred to three House committees, where it has sat without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and young adults up to age 26 who use insulin and are covered by private or employer-sponsored insurance. They would pay no deductible and no more than $35 per 30-day supply for at least one insulin product of each type (rapid-acting, long-acting, etc.) and dosage form their plan selects, and the same protections would reach them even inside catastrophic marketplace plans before the deductible is met.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young insulin users on private plans

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group and individual health plans from applying a deductible to selected insulin products for enrollees 26 or younger, starting with plan years in 2026.
Caps cost-sharing for those products at the lesser of $35 per 30-day supply or 25% of the negotiated net price, with the price calculated after rebates held by pharmacy benefit managers.
Requires the same coverage and cap inside catastrophic ACA plans before the deductible is met, and applies the rules to employer plans under ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group plans, who would absorb the difference between what patients pay and the insulin's cost. Some of that would likely be passed back into premiums, spread across all enrollees. Insulin manufacturers are not directly forced to cut prices; the bill caps what patients pay, not list prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and employers with group plans

drawbacks.text: Plans, not patients or regulators, choose which insulin products count as 'selected,' so a plan could satisfy the $35 cap by covering only cheaper insulins and keep applying higher cost-sharing to newer or pricier products.
The mandate raises costs for employers and insurers that sponsor group plans, which would likely be passed on to workers and premium-payers in some form; the bill contains no offsetting funding.
The cap applies only to people 26 and younger, leaving older insulin users on private plans subject to ordinary deductibles and cost-sharing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to young people with diabetes is concrete and immediate: no deductible and no more than $35 a month for a drug they cannot live without [S2]. The cost falls on insurers and employers, who would likely spread it across premiums, and on plans losing flexibility to steer patients to whichever insulin is cheapest. Whether the burden on employers is large is unclear, since the cap applies only to selected products for a limited age group. The main design weakness is that the plans themselves choose which products count as "selected," which could let them cover only cheaper insulins and leave patients on newer brand-name products facing higher cost-sharing [S2]. On balance, a modest, targeted consumer protection with a real but manageable cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and sent to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up since.

narrative.text: H.R. 2636 was introduced on April 3, 2025 by Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH).
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees — a three-way referral that requires any one of three committees to act.
No committee has reported the bill and no vote has been scheduled; there is no further action in the record.
It has 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers, employers, and pharmacy intermediaries are better off so far because no committee has moved to impose the insulin cost-sharing cap on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; no mandate took effect

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap insulin cost-sharing for people 26 and younger.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; the bill sits in committees controlled by the Republican majority with no action.

industries.note: Insurers could no longer charge deductibles or cost-sharing above the $35/25% cap on selected insulin products for young enrollees, absorbing the difference in plan cost. Smaller insurers with slim margins feel this most.

The bill's cost-sharing floor is calculated net of all price concessions, including rebates captured by pharmacy benefit managers, which forces rebate dollars to count toward lower patient costs but leaves the PBM intermediation model itself untouched and unregulated.

The bill lowers what patients pay out of pocket but does nothing to lower the manufacturer list prices that drive insulin costs; coverage mandates through private plans can actually guarantee a paying customer base.
ERISA plans face a new coverage mandate for young enrollees, adding cost, though limited to insulin for those 26 and under.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills with a single Democratic sponsor, no Republican cosponsors, and referrals to three committees die quietly without a markup or a vote, and that is the likely path here unless insulin costs become a legislative priority this session.
